mil2:1.2: Long ago, it seems, while the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa was still in force, a great Saṅgha of mendicants lived in a certain monastery near the Gaṅgā. There the mendicants, accomplished in observances and ethics, would rise at dawn, take their long-handled brooms, and, reflecting on the qualities of the Buddha, sweep the courtyard and make a heap of rubbish.
mil2:1.3: Then a certain mendicant addressed a novice: “Come, novice, throw away this rubbish”—
mil2:1.4: he said, but the novice went off as if not listening. And a second time …
mil2:1.5: Called a third time as well, he just went off as if not listening.
mil2:1.6: Then that mendicant, thinking, “How disobedient this novice is!”, became angry and struck him with the broom handle.
mil2:1.7: Then, weeping, and throwing away the rubbish out of fear, he thought: “By this meritorious deed of throwing away rubbish, until I attain extinguishment, in the meantime, in each place where I am reborn, may I be greatly powerful and greatly radiant, like the midday sun”—
mil2:1.9: Having thrown away the rubbish, he went to the Gaṅgā ford to bathe; and seeing the rushing surge of the Gaṅgā’s waves roaring, he thought: “Until I attain extinguishment, in the meantime, in each place where I am reborn, may I have ready eloquence that arises on the spot, inexhaustible eloquence, like this surge of waves”—
mil2:2.1: That mendicant, too, after putting the broom back in the broom shed, was going to the Gaṅgā ford to bathe when he heard the novice’s aspiration, and he thought: “Even though I was the one who put him to work, he aspires like this; why would my own aspiration not succeed?”—
mil2:2.2: and having thought it over, he made an aspiration: “Until I attain extinguishment, in the meantime, in each place where I am reborn, may I have inexhaustible eloquence like this surge of Gaṅgā waves; may I be able to untangle and unravel all the ingenious questions that he asks, each one as it is asked”—
mil2:3.1: Both of them, wandering on among gods and among humans, spent one interval between buddhas.
mil2:3.2: Then our Blessed One also declared of these two, just as the elder Moggaliputtatissa is foreseen, so too these two are foreseen: when five hundred years have passed after my final extinguishment, these two will arise; the Dhamma and Vinaya that I have taught in subtle form, these two will, by way of questions, similes, and reasoning, make free of tangles and thickets and will analyze.
mil2:4.1: Of those two, the novice became a king named Milinda in the city of Sāgala in Jambudīpa.
mil2:4.2: He was wise, accomplished, and intelligent, competent in counsel, application, arrangement, and action concerning the past, the future, and the present; when it was time to act he acted after careful consideration; and many treatises had been learned by him.
mil2:4.4: Revelation, tradition, enumeration, yoga, polity, the Vaiśeṣika, calculation, music, medicine, the four Vedas, the ancient lore, the histories, astronomy, sorcery, portents, counsel, warfare, and prosody, together with the Buddha’s word: nineteen. He was a sophist, hard to approach, hard to overcome, said to be the foremost among the many founders of sects. In all Jambudīpa there was no one equal to King Milinda in strength, speed, courage, and wisdom. He was rich, of great wealth, of great possessions, with boundless troops and vehicles.
mil2:5.1: Then one day King Milinda, wishing to see his array of the best troops, his army of four divisions with its boundless troops and vehicles, left the city and, having inspected the divisions of his army outside the city and had them paraded, that king—a loud talker, with a mind eager to plunge into discussions with Lokāyata sophists, confident and swaggering—looked at the sun and addressed his ministers—
mil2:5.2: “Sirs, much of the day still remains; what shall we do? If we enter the city right now, is there some wise ascetic or brahmin, with an order, with a following, a teacher of a following—even one who claims to be an arahant, a perfectly awakened Buddha—who is able to converse with me and dispel my doubt? We shall approach him, ask a question, and have our doubt dispelled.”
mil2:6.1: When this was said, the five hundred Yonakas said to King Milinda—
mil2:6.2: “There are, Great King, six teachers: Pūraṇa Kassapa, Makkhali Gosāla, the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta, Ajita Kesakambala, and Pakudha Kaccāyana. They have orders and followings, they are teachers of followings, well known, renowned, founders of sects, esteemed as good by many people. Go, Great King, ask them your question and have your doubt dispelled.”
mil2:7.1: Then King Milinda, surrounded by five hundred Yonakas, mounted a splendid chariot with a fine team and went to Pūraṇa Kassapa. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with Pūraṇa Kassapa; after exchanging courteous, memorable conversation, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, King Milinda said to Pūraṇa Kassapa—
mil2:7.4: “If, Venerable Kassapa, the earth protects the world, then why do beings who go to the Avīci hell pass beyond the earth as they go?”
mil2:7.5: When this was said, Pūraṇa Kassapa was unable either to swallow it down or to spit it out; he sat there silent, with his face downcast and his shoulders slumped, brooding.
mil2:8.1: Then King Milinda said to Makkhali Gosāla—
mil2:8.2: “Are there, Venerable Gosāla, skillful and unskillful deeds? Is there a fruit and result of deeds well done and badly done?”
mil2:8.3: “There are no, Great King, skillful and unskillful deeds; there is no fruit or result of deeds well done and badly done.
mil2:8.4: Those, Great King, who are aristocrats in this world will, even after going to the next world, again be aristocrats; those who are brahmins, merchants, workers, outcastes, and scavengers will, even after going to the next world, again be brahmins, merchants, workers, outcastes, and scavengers.
mil2:8.6: “If, Venerable Gosāla, those who are aristocrats, brahmins, merchants, workers, outcastes, and scavengers in this world will, even after going to the next world, again be just aristocrats, brahmins, merchants, workers, outcastes, and scavengers, then there is nothing to be done with skillful and unskillful deeds.
mil2:8.7: In that case, Venerable Gosāla, those in this world who have had their hands cut off will, even after going to the next world, again be just those with their hands cut off.
mil2:8.8: Those who have had their feet cut off will be just those with their feet cut off.
mil2:8.9: Those who have had their hands and feet cut off will be just those with their hands and feet cut off.
mil2:8.10: Those who have had their ears cut off will be just those with their ears cut off.
mil2:8.11: Those who have had their noses cut off will be just those with their noses cut off.
mil2:8.12: Those who have had their ears and noses cut off will be just those with their ears and noses cut off.”
mil2:9.2: “Jambudīpa is truly empty, sirs! Jambudīpa is truly chaff! There is no ascetic or brahmin who is able to converse with me and dispel my doubt.”
mil2:10.2: “How delightful, sirs, is this moonlit night! Which ascetic or brahmin should we visit today to ask a question? Who is able to converse with me and dispel my doubt?”
mil2:10.3: When this was said, the ministers stood silent, looking at the king’s face.
mil2:11.1: Now at that time, for twelve years the city of Sāgala had been empty of wise ascetics, brahmins, and householders. Wherever he heard that wise ascetics, brahmins, and householders were living, the king went there and asked them a question; and all of them, unable to satisfy the king with their answers, left for one place or another.
mil2:11.2: Those who did not leave for another direction all stayed silent.
mil2:11.3: As for the mendicants, most of them went to the Himalaya.
mil2:12.1: Now at that time a hundred crores of arahants were living on the Himalaya mountain at Rakkhitatala.
mil2:12.2: Then Venerable Assagutta, with his divine ear element, heard the words of King Milinda, and having assembled the Saṅgha of mendicants on the summit of Yugandhara, he asked the mendicants—
mil2:12.3: “Friends, is there any mendicant who is competent to converse with King Milinda and dispel his doubt?”
mil2:13.1: When this was said, the hundred crores of arahants were silent.
mil2:13.4: Then Venerable Assagutta said to the Saṅgha of mendicants—
mil2:13.5: “Friends, in the heaven of the Thirty-Three, to the east of Vejayanta, there is a palace named Ketumatī; a god named Mahāsena lives there. He is competent to converse with that King Milinda and dispel his doubt.”
mil2:14.1: Then the hundred crores of arahants vanished from Mount Yugandhara and appeared in the heaven of the Thirty-Three.
mil2:14.2: Sakka, ruler of gods, saw those mendicants coming from afar; and seeing them, he went to Venerable Assagutta, bowed to him, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka, ruler of gods, said to Venerable Assagutta—
mil2:14.3: “A great Saṅgha of mendicants has arrived, venerable sir. I am the monastery attendant of the Saṅgha. What is needed? What should I do?”
mil2:15.1: Then Venerable Assagutta said to Sakka, ruler of gods—
mil2:15.2: “There is, Great King, in the city of Sāgala in Jambudīpa, a king named Milinda, a sophist, hard to approach, hard to overcome, said to be the foremost among the many founders of sects. He approaches the Saṅgha of mendicants, asks questions in a spirit of dogmatic argument, and harasses the Saṅgha of mendicants.”
mil2:16.1: Then Sakka, ruler of gods, said to Venerable Assagutta—
mil2:16.2: “This King Milinda, venerable sir, passed away from here and arose among humans. This god named Mahāsena, venerable sir, lives in the palace Ketumatī; he is competent to converse with that King Milinda and dispel his doubt. We shall request that god for rebirth in the human world.”
mil2:17.1: Then Sakka, ruler of gods, placing the Saṅgha of mendicants in front, entered the palace Ketumatī, embraced the god Mahāsena, and said—
mil2:17.2: “The Saṅgha of mendicants requests you, dear sir, to be reborn in the human world.”
mil2:17.3: “I have no need, venerable sir, of the human world, which is rich in deeds; the human world is harsh. Right here, venerable sir, in the heavenly realm, being reborn in higher and higher places, I will be fully extinguished.”
mil2:17.5: Requested a third time as well by Sakka, ruler of gods, the god Mahāsena spoke thus—
mil2:17.6: “I have no need, venerable sir, of the human world, which is rich in deeds; the human world is harsh. Right here, venerable sir, in the heavenly realm, being reborn in higher and higher places, I will be fully extinguished.”
mil2:18.1: Then Venerable Assagutta said to the god Mahāsena—
mil2:18.2: “Here, dear sir, as we survey the world with its gods, apart from you we see no one else who is able to break King Milinda’s doctrine and uphold the dispensation. The Saṅgha of mendicants requests you, dear sir. Please, good man, be reborn in the human world and uphold the dispensation of the One with Ten Powers.”
mil2:18.3: When this was said, the god Mahāsena, thinking, “It seems I will be able to break King Milinda’s doctrine and uphold the Buddha’s dispensation,” became thrilled and delighted, elated and exultant, and gave his promise: “Good, venerable sir, I will arise in the human world.”
mil2:19.1: Then those mendicants, having completed that task in the heavenly realm, vanished from among the gods of the Thirty-Three and appeared on the Himalaya mountain at Rakkhitatala.
mil2:20.1: Then Venerable Assagutta said to the Saṅgha of mendicants—
mil2:20.2: “Friends, is there any mendicant in this Saṅgha of mendicants who has not come to the assembly?”
mil2:20.3: When this was said, a certain mendicant said to Venerable Assagutta—
mil2:20.4: “There is, venerable sir, Venerable Rohaṇa, who seven days ago entered the Himalaya mountain and attained cessation. Send a messenger to him.”
mil2:20.5: And Venerable Rohaṇa, emerging from cessation at that very moment—thinking, “The Saṅgha is waiting for me”—vanished from the Himalaya mountain and appeared at Rakkhitatala in front of the hundred crores of arahants.
mil2:21.1: Then Venerable Assagutta said to Venerable Rohaṇa—
mil2:21.2: “Friend Rohaṇa, as the Buddha’s dispensation is breaking up, do you not see what needs to be done for the Saṅgha?”
mil2:22.1: “In that case, friend Rohaṇa, perform a penance.”
mil2:22.3: “There is, friend Rohaṇa, on the slope of the Himalaya mountain a brahmin village named Gajaṅgala; there a brahmin named Soṇuttara lives. A son will be born to him, a boy named Nāgasena. So you, friend Rohaṇa, for seven years and ten months should enter that family for alms, take the boy Nāgasena out, and give him the going forth. As soon as he has gone forth, you will be released from the penance.”
mil2:23.1: The god Mahāsena also passed away from the heavenly realm and took conception in the womb of the wife of the brahmin Soṇuttara. Together with his taking of conception, three marvelous and wonderful things occurred: weapons blazed, the finest crops sprang up, and a great cloud rained down.
mil2:23.2: And Venerable Rohaṇa, from the time of his taking conception, for seven years and ten months entered that family for alms, and on not even a single day did he receive a spoonful of rice or a ladleful of gruel, or a bow, or a gesture of joined palms, or a mark of respect; he received nothing but abuse and insults—there was no one who spoke even the mere words “Move on, venerable sir.” But after seven years and ten months had passed, one day he did receive the mere words “Move on, venerable sir.”
mil2:23.3: On that very day the brahmin too, coming back from his work outside, saw the elder on the road and said, “Sir renunciant, did you go to our house?”
mil2:23.10: On the following day the brahmin sat down right at his house door, thinking, “Today I will rebuke the renunciant for a lie.”
mil2:23.11: On the following day the elder arrived at the brahmin’s house door.
mil2:24.2: “Yesterday, though you received nothing at our house, you said ‘We received it’. Is lying fitting for you?”
mil2:24.4: “At your house, brahmin, (…) for seven years and ten months we did not receive even the mere words ‘Move on’; yesterday we received the mere words ‘Move on’; so on account of that exchange of words we spoke thus.”
mil2:25.2: “These people, even on receiving a mere exchange of words, praise it in the midst of the people, saying ‘We received it’; why would they not praise it if they received some other solid or soft food?” Becoming confident, he had a spoonful of almsfood served from the meal prepared for himself, together with the accompanying curry, and said, “You will receive this almsfood at all times”—
mil2:26.1: From the following day onward, seeing the calm of the elder as he approached, he became even more confident, and he requested the elder to take his meal at his house at all times.
mil2:26.2: The elder consented by silence; day after day, when he had finished the meal and was leaving, he would speak a little of the Buddha’s word before going.
mil2:26.3: And in due course the brahmin’s wife too, after ten months, gave birth to a son; they gave him the name “Nāgasena”. He grew up gradually and became seven years old.
mil2:27.1: Then the father of the boy Nāgasena said to the boy Nāgasena—
mil2:27.2: “In this brahmin family, my dear Nāgasena, you should learn the studies.”
mil2:27.3: “What, father, are called the studies in this brahmin family?”
mil2:27.4: “The three Vedas, my dear Nāgasena, are called the studies; the remaining skills are called crafts.”
mil2:28.1: Then the brahmin Soṇuttara, having given a thousand as the teacher’s fee to the brahmin teacher, and having had a small bed laid out to one side in a chamber inside the mansion, said to the brahmin teacher—
mil2:28.2: “Please teach this boy the mantras, brahmin.”
mil2:28.3: “In that case, dear boy, learn the mantras.”
mil2:28.4: The brahmin teacher recited, and with just a single recitation the three Vedas of the boy Nāgasena went into his heart, became fluent on the tongue, well retained, well ordered, and well attended to; and at once the eye arose in him with regard to the three Vedas—with their glossaries and ritual, with phonology and analysis, with the histories as the fifth; he became expert in words, a grammarian, and perfect in the Lokāyata and the marks of a great man.
mil2:29.1: Then the boy Nāgasena said to his father—
mil2:29.2: “Is there, father, anything more to be learned in this brahmin family beyond this, or is this all?”
mil2:29.3: “There is nothing more, my dear Nāgasena, to be learned in this brahmin family beyond this; this is all that is to be learned.”
mil2:30.1: Then the boy Nāgasena, having completed his teacher’s instruction, came down from the mansion, his heart urged on by impressions from the past; gone to seclusion and withdrawn in solitude, examining the beginning, middle, and end of his own craft, and not seeing even a trifle of substance in the beginning, the middle, or the end, he thought: “Alas, how empty these Vedas are, sirs; alas, how these Vedas are chaff, without substance, without essence”—
mil2:31.1: Now at that time Venerable Rohaṇa, seated in the Vattaniya lodging, understood with his mind the thought in the mind of the boy Nāgasena. He dressed, took his bowl and robe, vanished from the Vattaniya lodging, and appeared in front of the brahmin village Gajaṅgala.
mil2:31.2: The boy Nāgasena, standing at his own gateway, saw Venerable Rohaṇa coming from afar, and seeing him, he was glad, uplifted, delighted, filled with joy and happiness—
mil2:31.3: “Perhaps this renunciant may know something of substance”—
mil2:31.4: he went to Venerable Rohaṇa, and having approached he said to Venerable Rohaṇa—
mil2:31.5: “Who are you, dear sir, looking like this, with shaven head, dressed in ochre?”
mil2:31.7: “Why are you called a renunciant, dear sir?”
mil2:31.8: “I drive out evil stains, and so, boy, I am called a renunciant.”
mil2:32.1: “Why, dear sir, is your hair not like that of others?”
mil2:32.2: “Seeing these sixteen impediments, boy, I had my hair and beard shaved off and went forth as a renunciant.”
mil2:32.4: “The impediment of adornment, the impediment of decoration, the impediment of oiling, the impediment of washing, the impediment of garlands, the impediment of perfumes, the impediment of scenting, the impediment of yellow myrobalan, the impediment of emblic myrobalan, the impediment of dye, the impediment of tying up, the impediment of combing, the impediment of barbers, the impediment of disentangling, the impediment of lice. When the hair is cut off, they grieve, grow weary, lament, beat their breast and weep, and fall into confusion. Entangled in these sixteen impediments, boy, people ruin all the most subtle crafts.”
mil2:33.1: “Why, dear sir, are your robes also not like those of others?”
mil2:33.2: “Clothes, boy, are bound up with sensual desire; the trappings and marks of householders are bound up with sensual desire. Whatever fears arise from clothing, those do not occur for one dressed in ochre; therefore my robes too are not like those of others.”
mil2:33.3: “Do you know the crafts, dear sir?”
mil2:33.4: “Yes, boy, I know the crafts; whatever mantra is supreme in the world, that too I know.”
mil2:33.8: “It is not the time, boy; we have entered among the houses for alms.”
mil2:34.1: Then the boy Nāgasena took the bowl from Venerable Rohaṇa’s hand, brought him into the house, and with his own hands served and satisfied him with fine solid and soft food; and when Venerable Rohaṇa had eaten and had taken his hand from the bowl, he said to him—
mil2:34.3: “When you, boy, are free of impediments and have had your mother and father give their consent, and you take on the guise of a renunciant that I have taken, then I will give it”—he said.
mil2:35.1: Then the boy Nāgasena went to his mother and father and said—
mil2:35.2: “Mother and father, this renunciant says, ‘I know the mantra that is supreme in the world’, but he does not give it to anyone who has not gone forth under him. I will go forth under him and learn that supreme mantra.”
mil2:35.3: Then his mother and father, thinking, “Let our son go forth and learn the mantra, and having learned it he will come back again,” gave their consent: “Learn it, son.”
mil2:36.1: Then Venerable Rohaṇa took the boy Nāgasena and went to the Vattaniya lodging, to Vijambhavatthu; having gone there, he stayed one night in the lodging at Vijambhavatthu, then went to Rakkhitatala; having gone there, he gave the going forth to the boy Nāgasena in the midst of a hundred crores of arahants.
mil2:36.2: And after he had gone forth, Venerable Nāgasena said to Venerable Rohaṇa—
mil2:36.3: “I have taken on your guise, venerable sir; now give me the mantra.”
mil2:36.4: Then Venerable Rohaṇa thought, “In which should I first train Nāgasena: the Vinaya, the discourses, or the Abhidhamma?”—
mil2:36.5: and having thought it over—“This Nāgasena is wise; he can learn the Abhidhamma easily”—he first trained him in the Abhidhamma.
mil2:37.1: And Venerable Nāgasena, with a single recitation, made fluent that entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka: the Dhammasaṅgaṇī treatise, adorned with triplets and couplets, beginning “Skillful qualities, unskillful qualities, undeclared qualities”; the Vibhaṅga treatise, adorned with eighteen analyses beginning with the analysis of the aggregates; the Dhātukathā treatise, divided in fourteen ways beginning with “Inclusion, non-inclusion”; the Puggalapaññatti treatise, divided in six ways beginning with “Designation of the aggregates, designation of the sense fields”; the Kathāvatthu treatise, divided by bringing together a thousand discourses, five hundred on one’s own side and five hundred on the opponent’s side; the Yamaka treatise, divided in ten ways beginning with “Root pairs, aggregate pairs”; and the Paṭṭhāna treatise, divided in twenty-four ways beginning with “Cause condition, object condition”—and he said: “Stop, venerable sir, do not recite again; with just this much I shall recite on my own”—
mil2:38.1: Then Venerable Nāgasena went to the hundred crores of arahants, and having approached he said to the hundred crores of arahants—
mil2:38.2: “Venerable sirs, I shall incorporate that entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka into these three terms, ‘Skillful qualities, unskillful qualities, undeclared qualities’, and recite it in full.”
mil2:39.1: Then for seven months Venerable Nāgasena recited the seven treatises in full; the earth resounded, the deities gave applause, the Brahmās clapped, and heavenly sandalwood powder and heavenly mandārava flowers rained down.
mil2:40.1: Then the hundred crores of arahants gave Venerable Nāgasena, at the full twenty years of age, full ordination at Rakkhitatala.
mil2:40.2: And after his full ordination, when that night had passed, Venerable Nāgasena dressed in the forenoon, took his bowl and robe, and, entering the village for alms with his preceptor, produced a thought of this kind: “My preceptor is truly empty, truly foolish, since, setting aside the rest of the Buddha’s word, he first trained me in the Abhidhamma.”
mil2:41.1: Then Venerable Rohaṇa, understanding with his mind the thought in the mind of Venerable Nāgasena, said to Venerable Nāgasena—
mil2:41.2: “Nāgasena, you have thought an improper thought; this is not proper for you, Nāgasena.”
mil2:42.1: Then it occurred to Venerable Nāgasena—
mil2:42.2: “How wonderful, sirs, how marvelous, that my preceptor knows with his mind the thought in my mind! My preceptor is truly wise. Let me ask my preceptor’s forgiveness.”
mil2:42.3: Then Venerable Nāgasena said to Venerable Rohaṇa—
mil2:42.4: “Forgive me, venerable sir; I will not think such a thought again.”
mil2:43.1: Then Venerable Rohaṇa said to Venerable Nāgasena: “I do not forgive you merely on this account, Nāgasena. There is, Nāgasena, a city named Sāgala; there a king named Milinda rules. He asks questions in a spirit of dogmatic argument and harasses the Saṅgha of mendicants. If you go there, tame that king, and make him confident in the Buddha’s dispensation, then I will forgive you.”
mil2:44.2: if, venerable sir, all the kings in all Jambudīpa came and asked me questions, I would answer them all and break them apart; but if, after I say ‘Forgive me, venerable sir’ and you say ‘I do not forgive’, then, venerable sir, with whom will I stay for these three months?”—he said.
mil2:44.3: “This Venerable Assagutta, Nāgasena, lives in the Vattaniya lodging. Go, Nāgasena, to Venerable Assagutta; having approached, bow with your head at the feet of Venerable Assagutta in my name, and say to him thus: ‘Venerable sir, my preceptor bows with his head at your feet and asks whether you are free of sickness and affliction, agile, strong, and living comfortably; venerable sir, my preceptor sent me to live with you for these three months’; and when he asks, ‘What is your preceptor’s name?’ you should say, ‘The elder named Rohaṇa, venerable sir’; and when he asks, ‘What is my name?’ you should say, ‘My preceptor, venerable sir, knows your name.’”
mil2:44.4: “Yes, venerable sir,” said Venerable Nāgasena, and having bowed to Venerable Rohaṇa and circled him with his right side toward him, he took his bowl and robe and, wandering on by stages, went to the Vattaniya lodging, to Venerable Assagutta; having approached, he bowed to Venerable Assagutta and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Venerable Nāgasena said to Venerable Assagutta—
mil2:44.5: “Venerable sir, my preceptor bows with his head at your feet, and says this: he asks whether you are free of sickness and affliction, agile, strong, and living comfortably; venerable sir, my preceptor sent me to live with you for these three months.”
mil2:45.1: Then Venerable Assagutta said to Venerable Nāgasena—
mil2:45.7: “My preceptor, venerable sir, knows your name.”
mil2:46.1: “Good, Nāgasena; put away your bowl and robe.”
mil2:46.2: “Very well, venerable sir,” he said, and having put away his bowl and robe, on the next day he swept the cell-compound and set out water for the face and a tooth-stick.
mil2:46.3: The elder swept again the place that had been swept, poured out that water and brought other water, and put aside that tooth-stick and took another tooth-stick; he did not exchange any conversation. Having done this for seven days, on the seventh day he asked again, and when it was again answered in just the same way, he gave permission to spend the rains retreat.
mil2:47.1: Now at that time a certain great laywoman had attended Venerable Assagutta for about thirty years.
mil2:47.2: Then, at the end of the three months, that great laywoman went to Venerable Assagutta, and having approached, she said to Venerable Assagutta—
mil2:47.3: “Dear son, is there another mendicant with you?”
mil2:47.4: “There is, great laywoman; there is a mendicant named Nāgasena with us.”
mil2:47.5: “Then, dear Assagutta, accept tomorrow’s meal together with Nāgasena.”
mil2:48.1: Then, when that night had passed, Venerable Assagutta dressed in the forenoon, took his bowl and robe, and, with Venerable Nāgasena walking behind as his attendant, went to the great laywoman’s residence; having approached, he sat down on the seat that had been prepared.
mil2:48.2: Then that great laywoman, with her own hands, served and satisfied Venerable Assagutta and Venerable Nāgasena with fine solid and soft food.
mil2:48.3: Then Venerable Assagutta said to Venerable Nāgasena, who had finished eating and had taken his hand from the bowl—
mil2:48.4: “Nāgasena, give the great laywoman a thanksgiving”; having said this, he rose from his seat and left.
mil2:49.1: Then that great laywoman said to Venerable Nāgasena—
mil2:49.2: “I am old, dear Nāgasena; give me a thanksgiving with a profound talk on the Dhamma.”
mil2:49.3: Then Venerable Nāgasena gave that great laywoman a thanksgiving with a profound talk on the Dhamma, transcendent and connected with emptiness.
mil2:49.4: Then, in that very seat, the stainless, immaculate vision of the Dhamma arose in that great laywoman—
mil2:49.5: “Everything that has a beginning has an end.”
mil2:49.6: And Venerable Nāgasena too, having given that great laywoman a thanksgiving, reflecting on the Dhamma that he himself had taught, and setting up discernment, while seated in that very seat was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
mil2:50.1: Then Venerable Assagutta, sitting in the pavilion, knowing that both had gained the vision of the Dhamma, gave his approval: “Well done, well done, Nāgasena! With a single arrow shot two great bodies have been split,” and many thousands of deities gave their approval too.
mil2:51.1: Then Venerable Nāgasena rose from his seat and went to Venerable Assagutta; having approached, he bowed to Venerable Assagutta and sat down to one side. To Venerable Nāgasena, seated to one side, Venerable Assagutta said—
mil2:51.2: “Go, Nāgasena, to Pāṭaliputta. In the city of Pāṭaliputta, at the Asoka monastery, Venerable Dhammarakkhita lives; learn the Buddha’s word in his presence.”
mil2:51.3: “How far is the city of Pāṭaliputta from here, venerable sir?”
mil2:51.6: Almsfood on the road is hard to get; how am I to go?”
mil2:51.7: “Go, Nāgasena; on the road you will receive almsfood: boiled sāli rice with the dark grains picked out, with many sauces and many curries.”
mil2:51.8: “Yes, venerable sir,” said Venerable Nāgasena, and having bowed to Venerable Assagutta and circled him with his right side toward him, he took his bowl and robe and set out wandering toward Pāṭaliputta.
mil2:52.1: Now at that time a financier of Pāṭaliputta was traveling on the road to Pāṭaliputta with five hundred carts.
mil2:52.2: The financier of Pāṭaliputta saw Venerable Nāgasena coming from afar, and seeing him, he went to Venerable Nāgasena, bowed to him, and said, “Where are you going, my dear?”
mil2:52.4: “Good, my dear; we too are going to Pāṭaliputta.
mil2:53.1: Then the financier of Pāṭaliputta, having become confident in Venerable Nāgasena’s deportment, with his own hands served and satisfied Venerable Nāgasena with fine solid and soft food; and when Venerable Nāgasena had eaten and had taken his hand from the bowl, he took a low seat and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the financier of Pāṭaliputta said to Venerable Nāgasena—
mil2:53.4: “Do you know, my dear, what is called the Buddha’s word?”
mil2:53.5: “I know, householder, sections of the Abhidhamma.”
mil2:53.6: “What a gain for us, my dear, how well we have gained! I too, my dear, am a student of the Abhidhamma, and you too are a student of the Abhidhamma; speak, my dear, the sections of the Abhidhamma.”
mil2:53.7: Then Venerable Nāgasena taught the Abhidhamma to the financier of Pāṭaliputta, and even while he was teaching, the stainless, immaculate vision of the Dhamma arose in the financier of Pāṭaliputta—
mil2:53.8: “Everything that has a beginning has an end.”
mil2:54.1: Then the financier of Pāṭaliputta sent about five hundred carts ahead and himself went behind; standing at a fork in the road not far from Pāṭaliputta, he said to Venerable Nāgasena—
mil2:54.2: “This, dear Nāgasena, is the road to the Asoka monastery. This, my dear, is our precious woolen blanket, sixteen cubits in length and eight cubits in width; please accept, my dear, this precious blanket out of compassion.”
mil2:54.3: Venerable Nāgasena accepted that precious woolen blanket out of compassion.
mil2:54.4: Then the financier of Pāṭaliputta, glad, uplifted, delighted, and filled with joy and happiness, bowed to Venerable Nāgasena, circled him with his right side toward him, and left.
mil2:55.1: Then Venerable Nāgasena went to the Asoka monastery, to Venerable Dhammarakkhita; having approached, he bowed to Venerable Dhammarakkhita and told him the reason for his coming; and in the presence of Venerable Dhammarakkhita he learned the Buddha’s word of the three baskets, with a single recitation, word by word in three months, and then in another three months attended to it as to meaning.
mil2:56.1: Then Venerable Dhammarakkhita said to Venerable Nāgasena—
mil2:56.2: “Just as, Nāgasena, a cowherd looks after cows while others enjoy the milk products;
mil2:56.3: so too, Nāgasena, though you bear the Buddha’s word of the three baskets, you do not share in the fruit of the ascetic life.”
mil2:56.5: In that very day and that very night he attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges; and together with Venerable Nāgasena’s penetration of the truths, all the gods gave their applause, the earth resounded, the Brahmās clapped, and heavenly sandalwood powder and heavenly mandārava flowers rained down.
mil2:57.1: Now at that time a hundred crores of arahants assembled at Rakkhitatala on the Himalaya mountain and sent a messenger to Venerable Nāgasena: “Let Nāgasena come; we wish to see Nāgasena.”
mil2:57.2: Then Venerable Nāgasena, hearing the messenger’s words, vanished from the Asoka monastery and appeared at Rakkhitatala on the Himalaya mountain in front of the hundred crores of arahants.
mil2:58.1: Then the hundred crores of arahants said to Venerable Nāgasena—
mil2:58.2: “This King Milinda, Nāgasena, harasses the Saṅgha of mendicants with debate and counter-debate and with putting questions.
mil2:58.3: Good, Nāgasena; go and tame King Milinda.”
mil2:58.5: if, venerable sirs, the kings in all Jambudīpa came and asked me questions, I would answer them all and break them apart. Go, venerable sirs, fearlessly to the city of Sāgala.”
mil2:58.6: Then the elder mendicants made the city of Sāgala glow with ochre robes and stirred it with the wind and counter-wind of sages.
mil2:59.1: Now at that time Venerable Āyupāla was living at the Saṅkhyeyya cell-compound.
mil2:59.3: “How delightful, sirs, is this moonlit night! Which ascetic or brahmin should we visit today for discussion and questions? Who dares to converse with me and dispel my doubt?”
mil2:59.4: When this was said, the five hundred Yonakas said to King Milinda—
mil2:59.5: “There is, Great King, an elder named Āyupāla, who knows the three baskets, is learned, and has mastered the transmitted scriptures; he now lives at the Saṅkhyeyya cell-compound;
mil2:59.6: go, Great King, and ask Venerable Āyupāla a question.”
mil2:60.1: Then a soothsayer sent a messenger to Venerable Āyupāla: “Venerable sir, King Milinda wishes to see Venerable Āyupāla.”
mil2:60.4: Then King Milinda, surrounded by about five hundred Yonakas, mounted a splendid chariot and went to the Saṅkhyeyya cell-compound, to Venerable Āyupāla. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Āyupāla; after exchanging courteous, memorable conversation, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, King Milinda said to Venerable Āyupāla—
mil2:60.5: “For what purpose, Venerable Āyupāla, is your going forth, and what is your highest goal?”
mil2:60.7: “Going forth, Great King, is for the sake of living by the Dhamma and living rightly; the fruit of the ascetic life is our highest goal.”
mil2:60.8: “But is there, venerable sir, any householder who also lives by the Dhamma and lives rightly?”
mil2:60.9: “Yes, Great King, there are householders too who live by the Dhamma and live rightly. When the Blessed One, Great King, set rolling the wheel of Dhamma at the deer park at Isipatana in Bārāṇasī, there was a breakthrough to the Dhamma for eighteen crores of Brahmās; and the breakthrough to the Dhamma of deities passed beyond the reach of counting. All of them were laypeople, not renunciants.
mil2:61.1: Furthermore, Great King, when the Blessed One was teaching the Mahāsamaya Sutta, the Mahāmaṅgala Sutta, the Samacittapariyāya Sutta, the Rāhulovāda Sutta, and the Parābhava Sutta, there was a breakthrough to the Dhamma for deities beyond the reach of counting. All of them were laypeople, not renunciants.”
mil2:61.2: “In that case, Venerable Āyupāla, your going forth is pointless; it is as a result of evil deeds done in the past that the Sakyan ascetics go forth and keep the austere practices.
mil2:61.3: Those mendicants, Venerable Āyupāla, who eat in one sitting must surely in the past have been thieves who carried off the possessions of others; having seized the possessions of others, as a result of that deed they now eat in one sitting, and do not get to eat from time to time; they have no ethics, no austerity, no spiritual life.
mil2:61.4: Those mendicants, Venerable Āyupāla, who live in the open air must surely in the past have been village-plunderers; having destroyed the houses of others, as a result of that deed they now live in the open air and do not get to use lodgings; they have no ethics, no austerity, no spiritual life.
mil2:61.5: Those mendicants, Venerable Āyupāla, who practice sitting only must surely in the past have been highwaymen; having seized travelers, bound them, and made them sit, as a result of that deed they now practice sitting only and do not get to lie down; they have no ethics, no austerity, no spiritual life”—he said.
mil2:62.1: When this was said, Venerable Āyupāla fell silent and said nothing in reply.
mil2:62.2: Then the five hundred Yonakas said to King Milinda—
mil2:62.3: “The elder is wise, Great King, but being not confident he says nothing in reply.”
mil2:63.1: Then King Milinda, seeing Venerable Āyupāla silent, clapped his hands, gave a shout of triumph, and said to the Yonakas—
mil2:63.2: “Jambudīpa is truly empty, sirs! Jambudīpa is truly chaff! There is no ascetic or brahmin who dares to converse with me and dispel my doubt.”
mil2:64.1: Then, as King Milinda looked over that whole assembly, seeing the Yonakas unafraid and not dejected, it occurred to him—
mil2:64.2: “Surely there must be, I think, some other wise mendicant who dares to converse with me, and that is why these Yonakas are not dejected.”
mil2:64.4: “Is there, sirs, some other wise mendicant who dares to converse with me and dispel my doubt?”
mil2:65.1: Now at that time Venerable Nāgasena—surrounded by a community of ascetics, with an order, with a following, a teacher of a following, well known, renowned, esteemed as good by many people; wise, accomplished, intelligent, subtle, discerning, clear-minded, disciplined, confident, learned, a master of the three baskets, a master of knowledge, with a penetrating intellect, a master of the transmitted scriptures, with the analytical knowledges fully developed, a holder of the texts in the Teacher’s nine-part dispensation, who had attained the far shore, skilled in teaching and penetrating the Dhamma and its meaning in the word of the Victor, of inexhaustible and varied ready eloquence, a speaker of colorful discourse, of excellent speech, hard to approach, hard to overcome, hard to cross, hard to obstruct, hard to repel; unshaken like the ocean, unmoving like the king of mountains; one who has abandoned strife, a dispeller of darkness, a maker of light, a great speaker, a crusher of the followings of rival teachers, a vanquisher of the adherents of other sects; honored, respected, esteemed, venerated, and revered by mendicants, nuns, laymen, laywomen, kings, and royal ministers; a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick; one who had attained the peak of gain and fame—displaying, before elders and wise ones endowed with attentive ears, the jewel of the Victor’s nine-part dispensation; pointing out the path of the Dhamma, bearing the lamp of the Dhamma, raising the sacrificial post of the Dhamma, performing the sacrifice of the Dhamma, upholding the banner of the Dhamma, raising the flag of the Dhamma, blowing the conch of the Dhamma, beating the drum of the Dhamma, roaring the lion’s roar, thundering with Indra’s thunder; satisfying the whole world with the great cloud of the ambrosia of the Dhamma, a cloud with sweet-sounding thunder, wrapped in a net of lightning of excellent knowledge, and laden with the water of compassion—had arrived in due course at the city of Sāgala, wandering on through villages, towns, and capital cities.
mil2:65.2: There Venerable Nāgasena was living at the Saṅkhyeyya cell-compound together with eighty thousand mendicants.
mil2:71.1: Then Devamantiya said to King Milinda—
mil2:71.3: There is, Great King, an elder named Nāgasena, who is wise, accomplished, intelligent, disciplined, confident, learned, a speaker of colorful discourse, of excellent ready eloquence, who has attained the far shore in the analytical knowledges of meaning, Dhamma, language, and ready eloquence. He now lives at the Saṅkhyeyya cell-compound. Go, Great King, and ask Venerable Nāgasena a question; he dares to converse with you and dispel your doubt.”
mil2:71.4: Then, as soon as King Milinda suddenly heard the sound “Nāgasena”, fear, terror, and goosebumps arose.
mil2:71.5: Then King Milinda said to Devamantiya—
mil2:71.6: “Does the mendicant Nāgasena, sir, dare to converse with me?”
mil2:71.7: “He dares, Great King, to converse even with the world guardians Inda, Yama, Varuṇa, Kuvera, Pajāpati, Suyāma, and Santusita, and with the great Brahmā, the father and grandfather; how much more with a human being!”
mil2:72.1: Then King Milinda said to Devamantiya—
mil2:72.2: “Well then, Devamantiya, send a messenger to the Reverend.”
mil2:72.3: “Yes, Your Majesty,” said Devamantiya, and sent a messenger to Venerable Nāgasena: “Venerable sir, King Milinda wishes to see you.”
mil2:73.1: Then King Milinda, surrounded by about five hundred Yonakas, mounted a splendid chariot and, together with a great force, went to the Saṅkhyeyya cell-compound, to Venerable Nāgasena.
mil2:73.2: Now at that time Venerable Nāgasena was sitting in the pavilion with eighty thousand mendicants.
mil2:73.3: King Milinda saw the assembly of Venerable Nāgasena from afar, and seeing it, he said to Devamantiya—
mil2:73.5: “It is the assembly, Great King, of Venerable Nāgasena.”
mil2:74.1: Then, as soon as King Milinda saw the assembly of Venerable Nāgasena from afar, fear, terror, and goosebumps arose.
mil2:74.2: Then King Milinda—like an elephant surrounded by rhinoceroses, like a nāga surrounded by garuḷas, like a jackal surrounded by pythons, like a bear surrounded by buffaloes, like a frog pursued by a snake, like a deer pursued by a tiger, like a snake that has met a snake-catcher, like a rat that has met a cat, like a ghoul that has met an exorcist, like the moon in the mouth of Rāhu, like a snake in a basket, like a bird in a cage, like a fish in a net, like a man who has entered a forest of wild beasts, like a yakkha who has offended Vessavaṇa, like a god whose lifespan has run out—frightened, agitated, terrified, shaken, his hair standing on end, dejected, miserable, bewildered in mind, his thoughts disturbed, and thinking, “May this retinue not despise me,” set up mindfulness and said to Devamantiya—
mil2:74.3: “Devamantiya, do not point out Venerable Nāgasena to me; I shall recognize Nāgasena without being pointed out.”
mil2:75.1: Now at that time, in that assembly of mendicants, Venerable Nāgasena was junior to forty thousand mendicants in front and senior to forty thousand mendicants behind.
mil2:76.1: Then King Milinda, looking over that whole Saṅgha of mendicants—in front, behind, and in the middle—saw Venerable Nāgasena from afar sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha of mendicants like a maned lion, free of fear and dread, free of goosebumps, free of fear and timidity; and seeing him, he knew by his bearing alone: “This is Nāgasena here.”
mil2:77.1: Then King Milinda said to Devamantiya—
mil2:77.3: “Yes, Great King, that is Nāgasena; you have recognized Nāgasena very well, Great King.”
mil2:77.4: Then the king was pleased, thinking, “Nāgasena was recognized by me without being pointed out.”
mil2:77.5: Then, as soon as King Milinda saw Venerable Nāgasena, fear, terror, and goosebumps arose.
